We are leading a nationwide Cluster Randomised Controlled Trial to evaluate the effectiveness of the Early Positive Approaches to Support (E-PAtS) programme—a parent/carer support intervention for families of young children with intellectual disabilities.
Learn more at epats-study.com




Funder: Sharland Foundation

Collaborators: University of Birmingham, Bangor University, Jigsaw School, Ulster University, University of Kent

This study aims to map the current landscape of Positive Behaviour Support (PBS) in the UK by gathering insights from professionals working across roles and sectors. The findings will inform the development of training and service models in the field.




Funder: Sharland Foundation

Collaborators: University of Birmingham, University of Warwick, Ulster University, Bangor University, Pyramid Educational Consultants

In collaboration with Pyramid Educational Consultants, I’m co-leading three linked projects focused on improving communication support for individuals with learning disabilities:

PECS Fidelity Tool
We are developing and validating a fidelity assessment tool for the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS), with the aim of standardising high-quality implementation in both clinical and research contexts.
See our background study
Pyramid Classroom Model Feasibility Study
This project explores the acceptability and feasibility of a class-wide communication-focused intervention designed for students with learning disabilities. The results will inform the design of a future randomised controlled trial.
PECS for Adults
We are investigating the feasibility and acceptability of using PECS with adults with learning disabilities—an area that remains under-researched but holds promise for improving communication outcomes in adult services.





Funder: GambleAware

Collaborators: Swansea University, University of Lethbridge, Swansea University Medical School, Reykjavík University

We are investigating the use of Contingency Management (CM)—a behavioural intervention commonly used in substance use treatment—as a novel adjunct approach for harmful gambling. Our recent study tested a remotely delivered CM programme, where participants received voucher-based incentives for abstinence, treatment attendance, and goal achievement. The findings show that CM is both feasible and acceptable in this context.
Read the study
Alongside this, we conducted a scoping review of gambling intervention research in the UK. The review identified relatively few studies, highlighting significant evidence gaps and the need for more UK-based evaluations of gambling treatment approaches.
Read the review

title: Richard J May PhD
text:
I am an Associate Professor of Behaviour Analysis at the University of South Wales (USW). My research work focuses on behavioural interventions and how they operate in real-world contexts, spanning areas such as learning disabilities, language development, gambling, and meta-science, with an emphasis on transparent and reproducible research practices.
I teach across undergraduate and postgraduate programmes in Psychology, Clinical Psychology, and Behaviour Analysis at USW, and I also teach a Behavioural Interventions course at Reykjavik University. I have a strong interest in how we can design learning environments that genuinely support students. I try to practice what I preach by applying behavioural principles to my own teaching materials. For example, I recently developed an open-access, web-based programmed instruction course to accompany my Behavioural Interventions class. The course uses active responding, immediate feedback, and structured sequencing to help students build fluency with the course material.
I also currently serve as an Editorial Board member for Perspectives on Behavior Science and the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, and I am the Co-Chair of the Teaching Skills sub-group within the Sharland Foundation Developmental Disabilities Applied Behavioral Research Impact Network.

title: Richard J May PhD
text:
I’m an Associate Professor of Behavioural Science in the Faculty of Life Sciences and Education at the University of South Wales. My research explores how behavioural interventions can be applied across diverse contexts and populations. From learning disabilities and language development to gambling and meta-science, my work aims to uncover what makes behavioural approaches effective in real world contexts —and ultimately, how they can create meaningful and lasting impact.
In addition to research, I teach on the Psychology, Clinical Psychology, and Behaviour Analysis programmes at both undergraduate and postgraduate levels.
I currently serve on the Editorial Boards of Perspectives on Behavior Science and the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behaviour. I am also a member of the Sharland Foundation Developmental Disabilities Applied Behavioral Research Impact Network, where I serve as Co-Chair of the Teaching Skills sub-group.

title: Talks
text:
Advancing Behaviour Analysis Through Open Science: Current Practices and Future Opportunities

Invited Address at the European Association for Behaviour Analysis Conference (2024)
 Science is currently undergoing an “open science revolution,” characterised by a push for greater transparency, accessibility, and reproducibility. This movement, driven by concerns over the so-called “replication crisis” and the need for more robust research practices, has led to widespread changes in how research is conducted, reported, and disseminated. Against this backdrop, this presentation examines the current state of open science practices within behaviour analysis, explores some the potential benefits of wider adoption. As part of this talk, I provide an overview of key open science initiatives, such as pre-registration, open data, and replication efforts, and explore at whether such practices have been embraced within our field. I conclude by offering some practical steps that behaviour analytic researchers, practitioners, and organisations might consider in order to integrate open science practices into their work. I will argue that by embracing open science principles, behaviour analysis can increase its rigor, expand its impact, and strengthen its position in the behavioural sciences and evidence-based practice.




A Critical Appraisal of Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses Published in Behaviour Analysis Journals

Experimental Analysis of Behaviour Conference, University of Chichester (2025)
 This talk examines the critical role of systematic reviews and meta-analyses in behaviour analysis, particularly their importance for evidence-based intervention selection and clinical decision-making. I outline key gold-standard methodological and reporting criteria for systematic reviews as evaluated by the AMSTAR-2 and R-AMSTAR assessment tools. Drawing on a comprehensive analysis of behaviour analysis journals, I present trends in both the prevalence and methodological quality of systematic reviews published in our field over time. The presentation concludes by identifying specific methodological and reporting deficiencies commonly observed in behaviour analytic systematic reviews and meta-analyses, offering recommendations for strengthening future research in this area.




No Alarms and No Surprises, Please: Challenges and Opportunities in Bridging the Research-to-Practice Gap in Behaviour Analysis

Invited Talk at the Experimental Analysis of Behaviour Group Conference, Bangor University (2023)
 The research-to-practice gap represents a disparity between the efficacy demonstrated in specific research contexts and the outcomes that are generated when interventions are applied in real-world scenarios. This presentation will outline some of the challenges that behaviour analysts may encounter in navigating this gap and will discuss insights garnered from recent research findings. This will include a discussion findings from SF-DDARIN projects exploring how well the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS) is understood and implemented in special education settings in the UK. The talk will include examples work from the field of Implementation Science, coupled with developments in open science and meta-science, and provide a reflection on how these domains hold relevance for behaviour analysts in effectively translating research into practice.

The talk will include examples work from the field of Implementation Science, coupled with developments in open science and meta-science, and provide a reflection on how these domains hold relevance for behaviour analysts in effectively translating research into practice.
